title: A trap after the book: calculate, then name the habit
outcomes: Calculates a reply when an odd move comes with a trap behind the natural reply
Says which opening habit the odd move broke
Tells a sacrifice that works from a look-alike that fails, by checking the position and not the pattern

steps.text: **An odd move: answer it or ignore it** sorted odd moves into threats and harmless ones. Some odd moves are neither: they invite your natural reply, and the natural reply is the mistake. When a capture or a developing move seems obvious right after an odd move, calculate it two moves deep before you play it. Ask what your move leaves loose and what it opens.

Now name the habit. In the position you just met, Black has moved the same knight three times (...Nf6, ...Ng4, ...Nxe5), brought the queen out and put a bishop on b4. Naming the habit tells you *where to look*: the knight that keeps moving and the king still in the middle. But a broken habit is not a refutation. *Rule of thumb:* name the habit, then calculate.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, two positions
steps.prompt: White's knight sacrifice on e5 after two different fourth moves by Black. Predict whether it works in each, then check.

steps.text: A trap works only in the position it was built for. The engine (depth 16) rates the same sacrifice at least four pawns worse after another black move (400 centipawns; 100 centipawns is about one pawn). A remembered pattern is a reason to calculate, never to play. *Rule of thumb:* the move that looks most natural, a capture or a developing move, is the one a trap punishes, so check what it leaves undefended.

steps.prompt: Choose one opening you play. Write the one odd move its opponents sometimes try, name the habit it breaks, and write the reply you would play. Check it in the Openings explorer or with the engine in My games.
